Automated Waste Classification using Convolutional Neural Networks¶

M507A - Methods of Prediction¶

Lijo Chacko¶

GH1040565¶

Business Context¶

One of the factors that must be developed in the current waste management sector is sorting waste effectively. The effectiveness of separating waste is critical in order to maximize the amount of waste that can be recycled. Separating waste prevents contamination of the waste, helps companies meet their obligations to environmental agencies, and enables the sale of high quality products through recycling. However, this process must not be manual since it is time consuming, hazardous to human life, and expensive.

Problem Definition¶

The purpose of this proposed project is to create an automated Deep Learning model that will be able to identify five different types of waste based on images of the waste. This will allow for increased efficiency, faster processing of waste, without sacrificing the quality of the waste separation, and therefore a reduction in labor costs for individuals performing the dangerous task of sorting waste.

Business Value¶

  • Operational Efficiency: These automatic systems do not suffer from fatigue, thus they can process many more pieces than a human would be able to in one day.
  • Cost Reduction: By taking the risk out of having employees perform hazardous work and by lowering the number of failed recycling batches due to incorrect identification.
  • Sustainability: Increased correct sortation allows the company to increase its compliance with governmental regulatory requirements.

Formulation as ML Task:¶

  • Type: Multi-class Image Classification

  • Input: Images of waste items

  • Output: Predicted class label (Glass, Plastic, Metal, Paper, Organic)

  • Model: Convolutional Neural Network (CNN)

Data Source¶

The dataset is sourced from the Waste Classification Dataset available on Kaggle.

https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/mostafaabla/garbage-classification

The unclean dataset contains approximately 15,000 images divided into 12 specific classes such as green-glass, brown-glass, white-glass, shoes, clothes.

Cleaning¶

Since the unclean dataset has 12 classes I will clean and merge some classes into 5 target categories by merging and ignoring unwanted categories. Objects in green glass, brown glass etc where all merged into one category Glass. Classes lilke bateries and shoes etc are ignored. Also reorganize the data and resize the images to laod for training

In [ ]:
base_dir = "garbage_classification/garbage_classification"
clean_dir = "clean_waste_data"

class_mapping = {
    'green-glass': 'Glass',
    'brown-glass': 'Glass',
    'white-glass': 'Glass',
    'plastic': 'Plastic',
    'metal': 'Metal',
    'paper': 'Paper',
    'cardboard': 'Paper',
    'biological': 'Organic'
}

if not os.path.exists(clean_dir):
    print("Creating clean dataset structure...")
    os.makedirs(clean_dir)

    for raw_cls, target_cls in class_mapping.items():
        src_path = os.path.join(base_dir, raw_cls)
        dest_path = os.path.join(clean_dir, target_cls)
        os.makedirs(dest_path, exist_ok=True)

        if os.path.exists(src_path):
            for img_name in os.listdir(src_path):
                src_file = os.path.join(src_path, img_name)
                dest_file = os.path.join(dest_path, f"{raw_cls}_{img_name}")
                shutil.copy(src_file, dest_file)
    print("Data cleaning complete!")
else:
    print("Clean data already exists. Skipping cleaning step.")

IMG_SIZE = (128, 128)
BATCH_SIZE = 32

print("\nLoading Data...")
data = image_dataset_from_directory(
    clean_dir,
    image_size=IMG_SIZE,
    batch_size=BATCH_SIZE,
    label_mode='categorical',
    shuffle=True,
    seed=123
)

class_names = data.class_names
print(f"Classes found: {class_names}")

Data Preprocessing¶

Normalizing the image pixels and splitting it to train the data

In [ ]:
normalization_layer = tf.keras.layers.Rescaling(1./255)
scaled_data = data.map(lambda x, y: (normalization_layer(x), y))

total_batches = len(scaled_data)
print(f"Total Batches: {total_batches}")

train_size = int(total_batches * 0.7)
val_size = int(total_batches * 0.15)
test_size = int(total_batches * 0.15)

remaining = total_batches - (train_size + val_size + test_size)
test_size += remaining

print(f"Splitting into:\n Training: {train_size} batches\n Validation: {val_size} batches\n Testing: {test_size} batches")

train_ds = scaled_data.take(train_size)
val_ds = scaled_data.skip(train_size).take(val_size)
test_ds = scaled_data.skip(train_size + val_size).take(test_size)

print("Data Preprocessing Complete.")

Total Batches: 206
Splitting into:
 Training: 144 batches
 Validation: 30 batches
 Testing: 32 batches
Data Preprocessing Complete.

Model Building¶

Building a Convolutional Neural network with three layesr of convolutions,batch normalization and pooling layers. This will then clasify the images into its 5 categories using Adam optimzer.

In [ ]:
model = models.Sequential()

model.add(layers.Conv2D(32, (3, 3), activation='relu', input_shape=(128, 128, 3)))
model.add(layers.BatchNormalization())
model.add(layers.MaxPooling2D((2, 2)))

model.add(layers.Conv2D(64, (3, 3), activation='relu'))
model.add(layers.BatchNormalization())
model.add(layers.MaxPooling2D((2, 2)))

model.add(layers.Conv2D(128, (3, 3), activation='relu'))
model.add(layers.BatchNormalization())
model.add(layers.MaxPooling2D((2, 2)))

model.add(layers.Flatten())
model.add(layers.Dense(256, activation='relu'))
model.add(layers.Dropout(0.5))
model.add(layers.Dense(5, activation='softmax'))

model.compile(optimizer='adam',
              loss='categorical_crossentropy',
              metrics=['accuracy'])

print("CNN Architecture Summary")
model.summary()

Defining the Callbacks function¶

Defining the special callback tools to monitor the training in real time. This 3 callbacks will save the models weigfht after every epoch, reduce the learning rate of the optimizer and set a timer to prevent overfitting.

In [ ]:
checkpoint = ModelCheckpoint(
    filepath='best_waste_model.keras',
    monitor='val_loss',
    verbose=1,
    save_best_only=True,
    mode='min'
)

reduce_lr = ReduceLROnPlateau(
    monitor='val_loss',
    factor=0.5,
    patience=3,
    verbose=1,
    min_lr=1e-5
)

early_stop = EarlyStopping(
    monitor='val_loss',
    min_delta=0.001,
    patience=5,
    verbose=1,
    restore_best_weights=True
)

print("Callbacks defined successfully.")

Callbacks defined successfully.

Model training¶

Training the CNN upto 50 epochs using the adam optimizer. With the timer set the automated tools will stop training if it stopped imporving and will save the best model. Also measuring the time taken to train the model.

In [ ]:
import time

start_time = time.time()

print("Starting Training...")

history = model.fit(
    train_ds,
    validation_data=val_ds,
    epochs=50,
    callbacks=[checkpoint, reduce_lr, early_stop],
    verbose=1
)

end_time = time.time()
duration = end_time - start_time

print(f"\nTraining Complete!")
print(f"Total Training Time: {duration/60:.2f} minutes")

Evaluating the Model¶

After training, I then evaluated my model using the test set that consisted of images that the model had never been exposed to prior to evaluation. I was able to measure the models ability to identify correctly when given images from outside of the training set. I have also generated a confusion matrix to view all possible error combinations.

In [ ]:
print("Evaluating on Test Data...")
test_loss, test_accuracy = model.evaluate(test_ds)

print(f"\nTest Accuracy: {test_accuracy * 100:.2f}%")
print(f"Test Loss: {test_loss:.4f}")

y_pred = []
y_true = []

for images, labels in test_ds:
    preds = model.predict(images, verbose=0)
    y_pred.extend(np.argmax(preds, axis=1))
    y_true.extend(np.argmax(labels.numpy(), axis=1))

plt.figure(figsize=(8, 6))
cm = confusion_matrix(y_true, y_pred)
sns.heatmap(cm, annot=True, fmt='d', cmap='Blues',
            xticklabels=class_names, yticklabels=class_names)
plt.xlabel('Predicted Label')
plt.ylabel('True Label')
plt.title('Confusion Matrix')
plt.show()

Conclusion¶

I built a Convolutional Neural Network to classify types of trash based upon image classification input. I improved my initial model through ten iterations of testing and made significant improvements. The final version of my model accurately identified unknown images at an extremely reliable rate. As such, the model represents a viable option for a computer-based automated recycling sorting method.

Overall Strengths of the Proposed Solution¶

Good Accuracy: The model has a good success rate for identifying the type of material at about 81% of the time. It is intelligent enough to identify the difference between tricky items, like a piece of paper versus a piece of fruit.

Smart Design: I used a unique building block called Batch Normalization. This allowed for faster learning, as well as avoidance of getting "stuck" on difficult images by the machine.

Safety First: This system is a huge win for worker safety. Since the computer does the identification, humans don't have to touch broken glass or dirty materials with their hands.

Simplified Data: The task was made easier for the model by grouping similar objects into fewer, but bigger classes, which works better for real recycling.

Limitations¶

Training Took Too Long: It took over an hour (76 minutes) to teach the model. This is because we used a regular computer. To do this quickly in a business, we would need faster, more powerful computers.

Messy Trash is Hard: The photos we used were clear and clean. Real trash is often crushed, dirty, or broken. The model might have trouble recognizing a soda can if it is completely flattened.

Background Problems: Our pictures had plain white backgrounds. A real factory has dark, moving conveyor belts. The model might get confused if the background looks too different from the training photos.

Future Work & Recommendations¶

  1. Start a "Human-Assisted" Pilot

Data: Our testing showed the model is 81% accurate. That is good, but it still makes a mistake on about 1 out of every 5 items.

Action: Deploy the system, but keep a human worker watching it. The computer does the hard work, and the human fixes the few mistakes. This keeps the workplace safe while the system learns to be better.

  1. Capture Multiple Angles

Data: he biggest improvement came when we rotated the pictures. This simple trick jumped our accuracy from 72% up to 88%.

Action: We should place cameras at different angles on the conveyour belt. This helps the computer recognize a bottle even if it is lying upside down or rolling around.

  1. Collect "Real-World" Samples

Data: This dataset consists of clean, single items on white backgrounds, which differs from real, dirty factory waste.

Action: We need to collect “dirty,” crushed, or wet images of garbage from actual waste bins. Training the model with images of the actual dirty waste will improve its performance in a true-world environment.

Deployment Recommendation¶

Decision: Yes, proceed to a Pilot Test.

I recommend deploying this model, but we should start with a small scale test run first.

Why to Deploy : Although the model has an 81% accuracy rate, it will be valuable to eliminate the need for humans to physically interact with hazardous objects such as broken glass or chemicals, which will increase worker safety right away.

During the Pilot Phase, a human supervisor should monitor the system. If the model incorrectly identifies an item, then the human can correct the models error. We can take the errors created during the Pilot Phase and retrain the model and increase its knowledge base.
